description: Growth conditions for microorganisms, high-risk foods, signs of spoilage and their uses in production.
content_html:
What Are Microorganisms?

Every time you leave a bowl of leftover chicken curry on the worktop overnight, you are giving microorganisms exactly what they need to multiply at speed. Microorganisms are invisible to the naked eye, but their effects — a furry grey patch on a bread loaf, a fizzing punnet of strawberries, the sour smell of yoghurt left too long — are very familiar. The three types you need to know are bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Each behaves differently and responds to conditions differently.

Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can divide roughly every 20 minutes under ideal conditions — meaning one bacterium can become millions in just a few hours. Yeasts are single-celled fungi that reproduce by budding and are responsible for fermentation (the process that makes bread rise and wine alcoholic). Moulds are multicellular fungi that grow as thread-like filaments called hyphae; you can see them on an over-ripe peach or a forgotten corner of bread.

What Microorganisms Need to Grow

Think of a microorganism’s needs as a simple checklist: food, moisture, warmth and time. Remove or limit any one factor and you slow or stop growth. This is the entire logic behind every food preservation and storage method you will study.

  • Food (nutrients): Bacteria and moulds thrive on protein and carbohydrates. High-protein moist foods — cooked chicken, shellfish, soft cheeses, cooked rice — are prime targets.
  • Moisture: Water availability (measured as water activity, aw) is critical. Dried foods like pasta, flour and biscuits have a very low aw, which is why they keep for months. Moist cooked foods have a high aw and spoil quickly.
  • Warmth: Most harmful bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 63°C — the temperature danger zone. Below 5°C growth slows dramatically; above 63°C most bacteria begin to die.
  • Time: Even in ideal conditions, it takes time for numbers to reach a dangerous level. A portion of cooked rice left at room temperature for two hours is much riskier than one left for twenty minutes.

Two additional factors affect growth: pH and oxygen. Most bacteria prefer a neutral pH (around 6.5–7.5). Very acidic foods like lemon juice or vinegar (low pH) slow bacterial growth — which is why pickling and marinating help preserve food. Some bacteria need oxygen (aerobic); others grow without it (anaerobic), which is why vacuum-packed meats can still carry a risk if temperature control fails.

Key Fact

Microorganisms need four things to multiply: food (nutrients), moisture, warmth (5°C–63°C danger zone) and time. Controlling any one of these slows or stops spoilage.

High-Risk Foods

High-risk foods are those that are ready to eat, moist and high in protein — meaning they support rapid bacterial growth and will not be cooked again before being eaten. The absence of that final heat treatment is what makes them dangerous: any bacteria already present will be consumed alive. Classic examples include cooked poultry, cooked rice, custards and cream-based desserts, soft cheeses, cooked shellfish and egg-based dishes such as quiche. A plate of leftover roast chicken that has been sitting at room temperature is a textbook high-risk food scenario.

Raw foods like uncooked chicken certainly carry bacteria (including campylobacter and salmonella), but cooking destroys those bacteria if the correct temperature is reached. The high-risk category refers specifically to foods that will be eaten without further cooking — so any bacteria present go straight into the body. A cooked chicken breast that has been left to cool slowly at room temperature is technically higher-risk than raw chicken that is about to go straight into the oven, because the cooked breast will be eaten as-is while bacteria multiply in the danger zone.

Enzymes and Food Spoilage

Enzymes are not microorganisms — they are biological catalysts produced by the cells of plants, animals and microorganisms themselves. In a freshly cut apple, enzymes called polyphenol oxidases react with oxygen in the air to produce brown pigments. This is enzymic browning, and it is why your apple slices turn brown within minutes of cutting. The same process causes bananas to go from yellow to brown and bruised pears to discolour.

Enzymic browning is not caused by bacteria or moulds — it is a purely chemical process. However, it is still spoilage because it affects the appearance, texture and sometimes the flavour of the food. You can control it by:

  • Acids: Squeezing lemon juice over cut fruit lowers the pH and deactivates the enzymes. This is why a fruit salad with a citrus dressing stays fresher-looking for longer.
  • Blanching: Briefly plunging vegetables into boiling water (blanching) denatures the enzymes by heat before freezing them. Without blanching, frozen peas or green beans would turn mushy and brown during storage because the enzymes would still be active even at –18°C.
  • Covering and minimising oxygen exposure: Wrapping cut fruit in cling film slows the reaction by limiting oxygen contact.
Key Fact

Enzymic browning is a chemical reaction controlled by enzymes — not by bacteria or moulds. Lemon juice (acid) and blanching (heat) are the two main controls. Vegetables must be blanched before freezing to prevent enzyme activity at –18°C.

Signs of Food Spoilage

Food spoils through three main routes: enzymic action, mould growth and yeast action. The signs are often obvious if you know what to look for.

  • Enzymic action: Ripening and softening of bananas (starch converts to sugars), browning of cut fruits and vegetables, softening of meat as proteases break down muscle fibres after slaughter.
  • Mould growth: Visible fuzzy patches (blue-green, white or black) on the surface of bread, soft cheeses, fruit and leftovers. Moulds produce thread-like hyphae and release spores; the visible fuzzy area is only the fruiting body — the hyphae may extend deeper into soft foods. Eating mouldy food is generally not recommended because some moulds produce toxic compounds called mycotoxins.
  • Yeast action: A fermenting, bubbling or fizzy quality, often with an alcoholic or sharp smell. This is why a punnet of squashed strawberries left in a warm kitchen develops a fizzing quality, or why opened fruit juice left for several days starts to ferment.

Not all microbial activity is harmful. Controlled use of microorganisms is at the heart of several traditional foods:

  • Moulds in blue cheese: Varieties such as Stilton and Roquefort get their characteristic blue-green veins from Penicillium mould cultures deliberately introduced into the cheese. The mould breaks down proteins and fats to create the distinctive strong, tangy flavour. The mould is controlled by specific temperature and moisture conditions during maturation.
  • Yeasts to raise bread: Baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) feeds on the sugars in bread dough and produces carbon dioxide gas and alcohol. The CO⊂2; is trapped by the gluten network in the dough, causing it to rise during proving. The alcohol evaporates during baking. Without yeast, bread would be dense and flat.
  • Bacteria in yoghurt and cheese: Lactic acid bacteria (such as Lactobacillus species) ferment the lactose in milk to produce lactic acid. This lowers the pH of the milk, causing the proteins to coagulate and thicken — producing yoghurt. The acidic environment also inhibits the growth of harmful bacteria, acting as a natural preservative. Hard cheeses use similar starter cultures alongside rennet to coagulate the milk proteins into curds.

Understanding that the same organisms that spoil food can also be harnessed to make it is an important distinction. The difference lies entirely in control: controlled conditions, starter cultures and careful monitoring of temperature, pH and moisture turn potential spoilage into valuable food products.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Explain question about food spoilage or enzyme control, students frequently lose marks by writing “keep it cold” or “use lemon juice” without explaining why these methods work. The command word “Explain” means “give reasons for and/or causes of” — so always link your method to a mechanism using ‘because’, ‘this means that’ or ‘as a result’. For example: “Blanching denatures the enzymes because the high temperature changes the shape of the enzyme’s active site, which means it can no longer catalyse the browning reaction” earns two marks on a 4-mark question; “Blanch the vegetables” earns nothing. For the distinction between enzymic browning and mould growth, be precise: enzymic browning is a chemical reaction driven by the food’s own enzymes; mould growth is a biological process involving living organisms. Muddling the two is a common error that costs marks on short-answer items.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are the three types of microorganism; they need food, moisture, warmth (5–63°C danger zone) and time to multiply — controlling any one factor slows spoilage.
  • High-risk foods are ready-to-eat, moist and high in protein; they are dangerous because no further cooking will destroy bacteria before the food is eaten.
  • The same organisms that spoil food — moulds (blue cheese), yeasts (bread), bacteria (yoghurt) — can be used beneficially under controlled conditions.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a high-risk food?
A. Dried pasta
B. Cooked chicken left at room temperature
C. Wholegrain bread in a sealed bag
D. Unprocessed oats
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B (cooked chicken left at room temperature). Dried pasta, sealed bread and unprocessed oats all have low water activity or will be cooked before eating; cooked chicken is moist, high in protein, and ready-to-eat — a classic high-risk food.

practice_questions.text: State two conditions that microorganisms need in order to multiply rapidly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct condition, up to 2 marks. Accept any two from: food/nutrients; moisture/water availability; warmth/temperature (within the danger zone, 5–63°C); time. Do not accept vague answers such as 'the right environment' without specifics.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during enzymic browning when a potato is peeled and left in the air.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: (1) enzymes in the potato (polyphenol oxidases) are exposed when cells are cut/damaged; (1) the enzymes react with oxygen in the air; (1) this produces brown pigments, discolouring the surface of the potato. A response that names the enzyme type and its substrate is not required at GCSE but would be credited if accurate.

practice_questions.text: Priya is making a fruit salad for a school event. She prepares it two hours before serving and notices the apple and pear slices have turned brown. Explain two methods Priya could have used to prevent this discolouration, and why each method works.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct method + 1 mark for the linked explanation, up to 4 marks total. Method 1: Add an acid such as lemon juice — because the low pH deactivates/denatures the browning enzymes so they cannot react with oxygen. Method 2: Cover/wrap the cut fruit tightly in cling film or place in water — because limiting contact with oxygen prevents the enzymic oxidation reaction. Other accepted methods: refrigerating the fruit (cold temperature slows enzyme activity); soaking in acidulated water. Each method must be paired with a 'because' explanation to gain both marks.

practice_questions.text: A small community bakery uses both yeast and a Penicillium mould culture in its production. Explain, with named examples, how each of these microorganisms is used beneficially in food production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two or three well-developed points for each microorganism, with accurate use of food-science vocabulary. Yeast explanation covers: feeds on sugars in dough; produces CO2 gas; gas is trapped by gluten network; dough rises during proving; alcohol evaporates during baking. Mould explanation covers: Penicillium introduced into cheese such as Stilton or Roquefort; breaks down proteins and fats; creates characteristic blue-green veins and strong tangy flavour; controlled by temperature and moisture during maturation. Correct named examples given for both.

Secure (3–4 marks): Both microorganisms addressed with some accurate science and at least one named example. Development is partial — may describe the process without fully explaining the mechanism.

Developing (2 marks): One microorganism addressed with some accuracy, or both addressed at a basic level with limited development. Limited use of technical vocabulary.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic statement about one use with little or no explanation (e.g. 'yeast makes bread rise').

practice_questions.text: Name the three signs of food spoilage recognised in food science.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming all three correctly: enzymic action (or enzymic browning), mould growth, yeast action. All three must be named for the mark. Partial credit is not awarded for this question.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following foods is NOT classed as a high-risk food?
Which microorganism is used to produce yoghurt?
Briefly plunging vegetables in boiling water before freezing is called _____, and it destroys enzymes to prevent browning.
Microorganisms multiply fastest between 5°C and 63°C, which is known as the temperature _____ zone.
Match each microorganism to its role in food production.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three types of microorganism relevant to food safety and food production?
flashcard_questions.a: Bacteria, yeasts, moulds — three distinct types, each behaving differently in food.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four conditions microorganisms need in order to multiply?
flashcard_questions.a: Food (nutrients), moisture, warmth, time — remove any one factor to slow or stop growth.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a high-risk food? Give one example.
flashcard_questions.a: A ready-to-eat, moist, high-protein food — e.g. cooked chicken or soft cheese.
A chemical reaction where enzymes in cut fruit/vegetables react with oxygen, causing brown discolouration.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must vegetables be blanched before freezing?
flashcard_questions.a: To denature enzymes that would otherwise cause browning and softening during frozen storage.

flashcard_questions.q: How does lemon juice prevent enzymic browning?
flashcard_questions.a: Its low pH deactivates the browning enzymes so they cannot react with oxygen.

flashcard_questions.q: Which microorganism is used to raise bread, and what gas does it produce?
flashcard_questions.a: Yeast; it produces carbon dioxide, which is trapped by gluten and makes the dough rise.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of bacteria is used in yoghurt production, and what acid do they produce?
flashcard_questions.a: Lactic acid bacteria; they produce lactic acid, lowering pH and thickening the milk.

flashcard_questions.q: Which mould is used in the production of blue cheese such as Stilton?
Name the three signs of food spoilage.
flashcard_questions.a: Enzymic action, mould growth and yeast action.

flashcard_questions.q: The temperature danger zone for bacterial growth is ___°C to ___°C.
Why do dried foods such as pasta spoil more slowly than moist cooked foods?
flashcard_questions.a: They have very low water availability (water activity), which limits microbial growth.

flashcard_questions.q: What visible sign indicates yeast spoilage on overripe fruit?
flashcard_questions.a: Bubbling or fizzing with an alcoholic or sharp smell — fermentation in action.

glossary_terms.definition: Microscopic living organisms — bacteria, yeasts and moulds — that can cause food spoilage or, in the case of pathogenic bacteria, food poisoning.
Ready-to-eat, moist, high-protein foods that support the rapid growth of pathogenic bacteria and do not require further cooking before being eaten.
Biological catalysts, usually made from protein, that speed up chemical reactions in food including ripening, browning and softening.
A chemical reaction in which enzymes in cut or damaged fruit and vegetables react with oxygen in the air to produce brown discolouration.
